import importlib.util, shutil

from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('pages',len(r.pages))
print('metadata',r.metadata)
texts=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    txt=p.extract_text()
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(txt)
    texts.append(f'\\n\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n\\n'+txt)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:2]))
PY"

strengths: The virtual-correspondence construction is a simple, useful contribution to geometric computer vision. It converts difficult four-point three-view problems into established 5-point/6-point and P3P solvers, offering an accessible approximate alternative to complex algebraic or homotopy methods.

The calibrated-camera results demonstrate meaningful practical benefits. In Table 2, 4p3v(M±δ)+R+F achieves PhotoTourism AUC@10 of 70.47 versus 70.54 for 5pt+P3P, with runtimes of 75.78 versus 105.50 ms. The faster 4p3v(M)+R+F also improves over the HC baseline in both accuracy and runtime.

Evaluation is substantial: 5,000 triplets per scene across PhotoTourism and Cambridge Landmarks, two RANSAC frameworks, fixed-iteration speed–accuracy curves, noise and outlier experiments, and an alternative metric covering all camera pairs. Holding out St. Peter’s Square for parameter selection strengthens the experimental protocol.

The manuscript clearly distinguishes approximate estimation from exact minimal solving and acknowledges scene dependence, small-overlap failures, and the limited benefit of learning after refinement. The supported calibrated-camera contribution provides a stronger case for acceptance despite the weaker extensions.
weaknesses: The unknown-focal-length extension has substantially weaker support. In Table 3, the best non-oracle variant reaches AUC@10 of 53.56 versus 56.79 for 6pt+P3P while taking 259.63 versus 11.72 ms; the inexpensive mean-based variants are less accurate still. Using four correspondences remains valuable, but no focal-length error is reported, and existing four-point HC methods receive no controlled accuracy comparison. Reliable calibration is therefore insufficiently established.

The geometric analysis provides limited guidance about reliability. Lemma 1 bounds point-to-line error by a potentially large triangle radius, without bounding pose error or the probability of obtaining a useful hypothesis from an all-inlier sample. The acknowledged scene dependence and noiseless approximation errors consequently remain difficult to predict. The manuscript also does not explain how adaptive RANSAC confidence accounts for such solver failures, although the fixed-iteration experiments mitigate concerns about the empirical comparison.

Learning contributes little demonstrated practical benefit after refinement: on PhotoTourism, 4p3v(L)+R obtains AUC@10 of 69.88 versus 69.90 for 4p3v(M)+R at approximately four times the runtime. Additionally, Equation 2 specifies a signed residual rather than a nonnegative Sampson loss; minimizing it as written need not reduce epipolar error. Whether this is a notation error or the implemented objective is unclear.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the straightforward central idea. Code availability is promised without a link, and absolute RANSAC inlier thresholds, the LM parameterization, and details of focal-length refinement are not specified sufficiently to reproduce the complete evaluation confidently.

A correctable reporting inconsistency warrants clarification: Table 9 gives identical accuracy and nearly identical RANSAC runtimes for corresponding M±δ and L±δ variants, whereas Table 10 reports substantially different individual solver costs. This weakens confidence in the learning ablation, without directly invalidating the calibrated mean-based results.
